claim: The Kymouse demonstrates full B-cell development competence.
source: In this study, we phenotypically characterised B-cell populations from the Intelliselect Transgenic mouse (Kymouse) demonstrating full B-cell development competence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phenotypic characterization data presented in the study, including flow cytometry analysis showing various B-cell populations.

claim: Kymice have CDRH3 length intermediate between mice and humans.
source: These differences result in Kymice having CDRH3 length and diversity intermediate between mice and humans.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data comparing CDRH3 lengths across species as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Kymice have CDRH3 diversity intermediate between mice and humans.
source: These differences result in Kymice having CDRH3 length and diversity intermediate between mice and humans.

claim: Kymouse naïve BCR repertoires are more human-like than mouse-like in their predicted distribution of CDRH3 shape.
source: To compare the structural space explored by CDRH3s in each species' repertoire, we used computational structure prediction to show that Kymouse naïve BCR repertoires are more human-like than mouse-like in their predicted distribution of CDRH3 shape.
evidence: This is supported by structural annotation and modeling data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The naïve Kymouse BCR repertoire is diverse with key similarities to human repertoires.
source: Our combined sequence and structural analysis indicates that the naïve Kymouse BCR repertoire is diverse with key similarities to human repertoires, while immunophenotyping confirms that selected naïve B cells are able to go through complete development.
evidence: This is supported by the combined sequencing and structural analysis data presented throughout the results section.

claim: Selected naïve B cells in Kymouse are able to go through complete development.

claim: The first immunoglobulin transgenic mouse was created in 1989.
source: Twenty-five years of progress in genetic engineering from the first immunoglobulin (Ig) transgenic mouse (Brüggemann et al., 1989) culminated in 2014 in the integration of a complete human Ig haplotype in mice for the first time (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Brüggemann et al., 1989.
